title: IP Addresses
objective: After this level you can explain how every device online gets an IP address, and why IPv4's 4.3 billion addresses ran out.
summary: Every device directly online has an IP address; IPv4 writes its 32 bits as four numbers from 0 to 255, allowing about 4.3 billion, and the free pool ran dry in 2011.

cards.headline: IPv4 had room for about 4.3 billion addresses. The central pool ran out in 2011.
cards.body: Every device directly connected to the internet needs its own address, the way every house needs one for mail to arrive. So how is an internet address built, and how did the world run short of numbers?

cards.headline: An address for the whole internet
cards.body: Level 31's MAC address only works on your local network. To cross the internet, a packet uses an IP address, from the Internet Protocol, first set out in 1981. Every device directly connected to the internet has one, and every packet's header carries two of them: where it came from and where it's going. It's the internet's postal address, written on every envelope.

cards.headline: Four bytes, written as four numbers
cards.body: An IPv4 address is 32 bits long. People write it as four 8-bit parts, each a decimal number, separated by dots: 128.9.0.32, for example. Each part is one byte, and Level 2's byte has 256 patterns, so each number runs from 0 to 255. All 32 bits together allow 4,294,967,296 addresses, about 4.3 billion.

cards.fact: On February 3, 2011, IANA handed out the last free blocks in its central pool of IPv4 addresses.
cards.context: IANA, which manages the world's pool of addresses, gave its final blocks to the five regional internet registries, which kept handing out their remaining stock within their regions for years. The long-term fix is IPv6, whose addresses are 128 bits: 96 bits more than IPv4. Since each extra bit doubles the count, IPv6 allows a number of addresses 39 digits long.

questions.prompt: An IPv4 address is _____ bits long.

options.rationale: That is one of its four parts.
That is a MAC address's length.

questions.explanation: An IPv4 address is 32 bits, written as four 8-bit parts.

questions.prompt: Match each kind of network address with its length in bits.
questions.explanation: A MAC address is 48 bits, an IPv4 address is 32 bits, and IPv6 addresses are 128 bits.

questions.prompt: Why can no part of an IPv4 address like 128.9.0.32 be higher than 255?

options.label: Each part is one byte, and a byte has 256 patterns, 0 to 255
Routers are built unable to handle numbers past 255
options.rationale: The limit comes from the size of each part.

options.label: Numbers above 255 are held back for secret uses
options.rationale: They simply cannot fit in 8 bits.

options.label: Only 255 countries are allowed internet addresses
options.rationale: The limit has nothing to do with geography.

questions.explanation: Each of the four parts is 8 bits, and an 8-bit byte has 256 patterns: 0 through 255.
